transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-05-03 15:00 PST
Duration: ~85 minutes
Attendees: Maya, Ethan, Lena (Redwood); Rajiv, Sofia, Tom (Peregrine)

Summary: high level deep dive into private VPC egress options, split-hop routing across subnets, NAT hairpin and scaling, DNS resolver behavior, and how kv-cache and batching interact with cross-AZ latency. Plan for an in-lab pilot and benchmark matrix.

Topics: PrivateLink vs NAT egress; split-hops between inference subnets and egress subnets; DNS resolver cache TTLs and split-horizon; KV cache locality; batching/quantization tradeoffs; perf test plan.

Action items (recorded in transcript for context): see metadata action_items.

Transcript: 
[00:00:00] Maya: all right thanks everyone for joining, i know we're all tight on time so we'll try and cover the topology and then go into kv cache and batching effects, um that okay with you all?
[00:00:12] Tom: yep that's good, mostly here to understand risk and timelines, and where latency might blow up when we go multi-az.
[00:00:20] Rajiv: also need to know the NAT sizing, we've got spikes up to 18k concurrent connections during peak telematics windows, so that is the big one for us.
[00:00:32] Ethan: cool, i'll start with a quick sketch of the network topology we recommend, and then we'll zoom into the egress patterns. sorry if some labels are off in the diagram, i screen shared and the overlay sometimes messes up.
[00:00:47] Speaker 3: (inaudible)
[00:00:50] Ethan: so imagine three inference subnets (az-a, az-b, az-c) hosting model nodes. requests come in via private link from your app plane into the inference ENIs. for egress we see two patterns: 1) centralized NAT GW per AZ with hairpin for control plane traffic, or 2) PrivateLink egress to an appliance/peering in your environment — the latter reduces public egress but adds routing complexity.
[00:01:15] Sofia: when you say hairpin do you mean source/destination check disabled on ENI and route table looping back to the nat? sometimes that kills the path because of asymmetric return routes.
[00:01:27] Lena: yeah good call, source/destination needs toggling on our side for the hairpin case; otherwise the keepalive to the resolver will time out and the kv-cache warm paths will break.
[00:01:36] Rajiv: our concern is packet wall time; if we do cross-AZ kv-cache misses and the runtime has to go to disk or to another AZ, the p50 jumps. we saw p50 go from 45ms to 120ms in a small test.
[00:01:50] Ethan: exactly, kv-cache locality matters. our recommendation for Private VPC is to collocate the prefix/KV cache in the same AZ as the serving node whenever possible, because cross-AZ RPCs are the dominant latency multiplier for token generation.
[00:02:05] Maya: can you quantify that tradeoff? like small model + batch 1 vs large model + batching? numbers help the procurement folks.
[00:02:13] Ethan: rough numbers we've seen on NVIDIA A100-ish infra: local kv-cache miss penalty ~2-4ms for local memory ops, cross-AZ gRPC call adds 30-70ms depending on the cloud egress path and DNS resolution. with batching you amortize the overhead, so throughput improves but latency p95 can still be high if a single request waits on a cold kv-cache.
[00:02:35] Sofia: about DNS: our resolver (shared VPC resolver) has a 60s TTL on private endpoints, but we use split-horizon for internal amazonaws endpoints; sometimes clients resolve to an internal lb IP that isn't routable from the inference subnet, we've tripped that a few times.
[00:02:50] Ethan: yeah that's a classic. our runbook suggests explicit Route53 resolver rules or conditional forwarding so inference nodes hit the right IP. also ensure that the resolver's EDNS and TCP fallback are allowed through your egress firewall — we saw retransmits inflate latency.
[00:03:06] Rajiv: on PrivateLink, does the runtime maintain TLS/mTLS into the linked service? and is SNI preserved for multiplexing?
[00:03:15] Lena: from our tests, PrivateLink preserves TLS but you need to handle SNI at the appliance if you're doing multi-tenant hostnames. MTLS is supported but requires cert provisioning on both sides; Redwood supports automated cert rotation if you want us to manage, otherwise we can hand off CSR instructions.
[00:03:34] Tom: ok rotation is fine but we need to keep keys in our HSM for compliance. is there an option for customer-managed KMS?
[00:03:42] Maya: yes, Private has integrations with customer KMS/HSM. that means the runtime has no plaintext keys in Redwood-managed vaults. we'll include that in the runbook.
[00:03:50] Sofia: back to nat sizing — our NAT GW is autoscaling but peeks at 25Gbps, and we have occasional connection storms from OTA updates. if the NAT saturates, what failover mechanism does Redwood suggest?
[00:04:03] Ethan: we usually recommend a multi-subnet egress design with per-az NAT plus an egress-proxy layer that can circuit-break and reroute to a fallback egress region or a cached stub. For time-critical inference calls, we also recommend an in-network caching tier — short TTL prefix cache to serve model-control calls without leaving AZ.
[00:04:24] Rajiv: would that require custom route table changes? we prefer to avoid manual interventions in prod.
[00:04:29] Maya: we can automate route flips via SSM runbooks — Redwood ops can coordinate automation to fail traffic to a standby egress if health checks fail. we'll show an example playbook.
[00:04:40] Ethan: ok now batching + quantization: quantized models reduce token compute time but increase memory bandwidth and can change KV cache size. aggressive 4-bit quantization gained us 2-3x throughput on some matrix ops, but in small context windows with many short requests you lose because tokenize and dequant cost outweigh throughput gains.
[00:04:59] Sofia: curious — how does quantization affect the KV cache format? do you store dequantized embeddings or compressed tokens?
[00:05:06] Ethan: good question. we keep the cache in raw, model-native format where possible to avoid dequant hops: i.e., the KV cache is in the representation used by the inference kernel. with q4 formats that means smaller memory footprint but care with alignment and padding. cross-AZ replication requires serialization which can add ~2-6ms if we gzip the payload; without compression it's cheaper but more bandwidth.
[00:05:28] Rajiv: so for our use-case (many short telemetry prompts per vehicle) sounds like we should favor lower quantization for p95 and keep kv-cache local, is that fair?
[00:05:36] Ethan: yes, for chatty short requests prefer minimal quantization and local caches, plus smart batching on the server side: request coalescing with a 5-10ms micro-batch window often yields best tradeoffs.
[00:05:47] Tom: what's the impact of micro-batching on latency jitter? some of our user interactions are latency-sensitive and can't have >100ms spikes.
[00:05:54] Ethan: micro-batching introduces queuing delay but can be bounded; in our experiments a 10ms micro-batch increased median latency by ~8-12ms but improved tail stability and throughput. we provide adaptive batching policies: latency-first (tight windows), or throughput-first (larger windows).
[00:06:08] Speaker 2: (crosstalk)
[00:06:12] Maya: ok let's drill into the bench plan: we propose a 4x4 matrix across az-local vs cross-az kv-cache, q8 vs q4, and batch window [0ms,10ms]. we'll run 30-minute soak tests and capture p50/p95/p99 and token-cost.
[00:06:27] Rajiv: can you also include DNS stress tests? last time we saw resolver failover cause 200ms spikes under load.
[00:06:33] Ethan: yes add DNS and also route flapping simulation where we force a NAT path change mid-soak.
[00:06:40] Sofia: about metrics — do you instrument token-level traces? we need to correlate our app-side request id to token spans.
[00:06:46] Lena: Redwood runtime emits per-request trace ids and kv-cache hit/miss counters; we can push that into your tracing backend via Datadog/OTLP. note that enabling full token traces increases payload size and slightly raises latency.
[00:06:59] Maya: small note — for compliance we'll redact PII on our side but we can pass raw traces over a dedicated PrivateLink to your observability stack if you prefer.
[00:07:09] Tom: yes that's a requirement, we can't allow logs into Redwood's hosted telemetry. private observability is a must.
[00:07:15] Ethan: for that we'll configure an egress endpoint that forwards traces to your collector over mTLS inside the VPC. works with PrivateLink.
[00:07:23] Rajiv: switching mode: what about KV cache warm strategies? pre-warm vs lazy fetch?
[00:07:30] Ethan: pre-warm is useful if you have predictable prompt prefixes — we can seed KV caches during deployment time. lazy fetch is when the runtime requests remote cache on a miss; combine with async prefetch to reduce p95. pre-warm costs more memory but reduces first-token latency.
[00:07:45] Sofia: and if we run cross-az pre-warm replication, what's the bandwidth cost? we have limited inter-az throughput budget.
[00:07:52] Ethan: replication bandwidth depends on model size and context window. for 2k context window we saw replication of ~30-80MB per model per sync. we recommend delta syncs and compressing with snappy for speed; full shims are heavy.
[00:08:06] Maya: quick interruption — Rajiv said earlier you hit 120ms p50 in your mini-test; can you describe the test so we can replicate it?
[00:08:14] Rajiv: yeah we ran a 3-node cluster across two AZs with NAT GW centralized, and the runtime had cross-az KV miss for about 15% of requests; that coincided with a DNS resolver TTL expiry and a NAT burst, so the added latency stacked. single AZ runs were ~48ms p50.
[00:08:29] Ethan: that aligns with our expectations. in that scenario we'd propose either localizing cache or adding a tiny edge cache per AZ and aggressive DNS resolver rules to avoid the TTL expiry race.
[00:08:40] Sofia: can you outline the config flags we'd need to flip on Redwood Dedicated? like kv_cache.prefer_local, batch.window_ms, quantization.level?
[00:08:49] Ethan: yes the flags are: runtime.kv_cache.mode = local|replicate|hybrid; runtime.kv_cache.repl_compression = snappy|none; runtime.batch.window_ms = integer; runtime.quant.level = q8|q4|fp16; runtime.network.egress_mode = nat|privatelink|proxy. we'll share the full list in the runbook.
[00:09:05] Lena: also include metrics toggles: runtime.metrics.token_tracing = on|off and runtime.tracing.destination = collector-url.
[00:09:12] Maya: let's capture security questions: SSO, RBAC, audit logs retention. Tom?
[00:09:18] Tom: we need 12 months audit logs, SAML SSO, role-based access, and the ability to export audit logs to our Splunk. performance-wise that shouldn't be affected but it's a compliance hard requirement.
[00:09:28] Maya: Redwood Private supports audit log export and SAML; we'll note retention options and an export example.
[00:09:34] Rajiv: one more operational ask — when you do failover route flips, how do you preserve active connections to the model? tokens in flight shouldn't drop.
[00:09:42] Ethan: we implement graceful drain with connection handoff using sticky session affinity and stateful transfer for short-lived kv-cache shards. in worst case some in-flight tokens are retried by the client automatically with idempotency keys. we'll show our retry semantics.
[00:09:56] Speaker 1: (laughs)
[00:09:59] Maya: ok nearing the end — recap: 1) run the 4x4 benchmark matrix in lab, 2) Peregrine to share topology and nat targets, 3) Redwood to send runbook and flag list, and 4) schedule pilot week.
[00:10:12] Tom: that works. two asks — ensure the pilot doesn't touch prod keys and provide a no-ops test that simulates OTA bursts.
[00:10:20] Lena: we'll do that — keys in test KMS and simulated connection storms for NAT.
[00:10:24] Maya: perfect. any final q's?
[00:10:28] Sofia: just one — what about cost delta for multi-az local caches vs centralized?
[00:10:33] Ethan: rough math: adding per-az cache nodes increases infra by ~20-30% but reduces egress charges and latent tails; for high request counts you'll often see net cost-neutral or savings due to fewer cross-az data transfers. we'll put a cost model in the follow-up.
[00:10:48] Rajiv: thanks all.
[00:10:50] Maya: thanks everyone we will follow up with the runbook and the bench plan.

(End of recorded extract — meeting continued with detailed config walkthrough and shared screen examples; notes truncated)
